approbation accorded to such self-evidently lightweight and inferior contemporaries as
Henry Hart Milman and Barry Cornwall (L ii 289–90; see notes to Preface). These aspects
of S.’s gathering thoughts and ideas for an elegy on Keats would of course have coincided
with other recent contexts: DP, with its high and abstract claims for the permanent power
and significance of poetry in the widest sense, had been written in February, in response to
Peacock’s argument that poetry had lost its importance for modern society; the quarrel with
Southey, and growing evidence of a concerted politically motivated public campaign to
destroy S.’s reputation; the decision to publish his most recent major poem, Epipsychidion,
anonymously in order to ‘avoid the malignity of those who turn sweet food into poison’ (L
ii 263); and the apparent conjunction of seriously failing health with personal unhappiness
and artistic failure.
